ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: In the circuit shown in the figure, after switch S is closed, due to a short-circuit or open-circuit fault occurring in a resistor element, the readings of both the voltmeter and the ammeter increase. Then which of the following faults may have occurred (　　)

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: In the circuit shown in the figure, after switch S is closed, if a certain resistor element has a short-circuit or open-circuit fault, and the readings of both the voltmeter and the ammeter increase, then what fault may have occurred?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: in the figure, the left side is a common node; the upper branch has ammeter A and resistor R1 in sequence, and the middle branch has resistor R2; the R1 branch and the R2 branch join at the middle-right node, so R1 and R2 are in a parallel relationship. After joining, it then passes through the right-side resistor R3 to the right-side common node, so after R1 and R2 are connected in parallel, they are connected in series with R3. Voltmeter V is connected between the middle node and the right-side node, that is, it measures the voltage across R3; ammeter A is connected in series in the R1 branch, measuring the current in the R1 branch. At the bottom there is a power supply and switch S. Then reason the influence of the faults: after switch S is closed, if R1 is open-circuited, then the R1 branch has no current, and the reading of ammeter A becomes 0, which does not conform to “the ammeter reading increases.” If R2 is short-circuited, then the parallel part is short-circuited, the voltage across the two ends of the R1 branch tends to 0, and the current in A decreases or is 0, which does not conform. If R2 is open-circuited, then the equivalent resistance of the parallel part increases, the total resistance increases, the total current will not increase, and the voltage across R3 also will not increase, which does not conform. If R3 is short-circuited, then the voltmeter measures the voltage across R3, and the reading becomes 0, which does not conform. If R3 is open-circuited, then the series main circuit is opened, and the total current does not increase, which also does not conform. If R1 is short-circuited, then the upper branch where R1 is located approximately becomes a wire branch, the equivalent resistance of the R1 and R2 parallel part decreases significantly, the total resistance decreases, and the total current increases; therefore the voltage across R3 increases, and the voltmeter reading increases. At the same time, ammeter A is in the short-circuit branch, and the current flowing through A also increases. Therefore the possible fault is an R1 short circuit.
